questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] a reminder pipeline at 15x under provider limits and outages (organized-build-scedulingpyjs, ARCHITECTURE.md). Scenario: the product grows to 5,000 salons booking 600,000 appointments a week, each owed a confirmation and two reminders. The email and SMS provider accepts at most 200 messages a second and bills per message. Appointments cluster on the hour, so in the largest time zone about 30,000 one-hour reminders for 09:00 visits fall due at 08:00. SMS may not be sent between 21:00 and 08:00 in the customer's local time. Last month the provider was down for two hours overnight. Write your design before you look: the weekly volume and the peak you size for, how worker concurrency is held under the provider's cap, how the 08:00 spike is flattened, which messages go first when the system is behind, how quiet hours are enforced and with what data, and how the backlog drains after an outage. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] Size for the peak, not the average: 600,000 appointments times three messages is 1.8M a week, about 3 a second on average, but the 08:00 wave alone is 30,000 sends, 150 seconds of work even at the full cap; the worker that would do it is constructed with no concurrency or rate-limit options, so it handles one job at a time per process.

[w3] The cap is enforced once, at the queue, not per process: a shared limiter of 200 jobs per second across all workers means adding workers raises throughput up to the cap and never past it; there is no worker process to tune yet, since the deploy notes still ask for an entry file that starts one.

[w3] Flatten the spike with a tolerance window: a row today carries one exact instant, so give each one-hour reminder a deterministic offset inside, say, the ten minutes before its nominal time (hashed from the appointment id); 30,000 spread over ten minutes is 50 a second, a quarter of the cap.

[w3] Priority needs a field the schema lacks: both reminders are typed simply as a reminder, told apart only by their instant, so the design adds a reminder kind and a priority (confirmations, then one-hour, then 24-hour) and feeds separate lanes or job priorities from it.

[w3] Quiet hours need a channel, a phone number and the customer's zone: notifications go to an email address only, while the customer profile holds an optional phone and an optional timezone, so SMS rows carry a channel, an SMS due inside 21:00-08:00 local is held until 08:00 or switched to email, and a profile with no zone falls back to the timezone the appointment itself records.

[w2] The drain needs a status that means 'try again': the statuses are pending, sent, failed and cancelled, so an outage today turns every send into a final failure; with a retry state and a backoff time, the backlog drains at the cap minus the live arrival rate, highest priority first, and a 24-hour reminder overtaken by its one-hour sibling is cancelled rather than sent.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — the first busy Monday at the new volume. The provider starts answering 429 halfway through the 08:00 wave; the held overnight SMS are released at 08:00 at the same moment as the weekly job that extends recurring series; and at the top of the hour two zones' waves overlap at the cap while a single first-in-first-out lane sends 24-hour reminders ahead of one-hour reminders for visits starting within the hour. What breaks, how does each problem show up, and what in your design prevents it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] Every 429 becomes a lost reminder: any error from the send call takes the failure path that writes a final status, and nothing reads failed rows again, so a capacity problem turns straight into thousands of reminders that never go out, and adding workers loses more. Provider replies must be classified: 429 and 5xx go back with a delay, a bad address fails for good.

[w2] A 429 speaks for the whole account, not for one job: the queue is created with no default job options, so nothing backs off globally; pause the shared limiter for the provider's Retry-After instead of letting each job retry on its own clock, and remember that a send retried after a timeout may already have been delivered, so the provider needs a deduplication key or the retry doubles a reminder.

[w3] The 08:00 pile-up is a scheduling choice: the series-extension job is still a placeholder that only logs, so nothing forces it to run at 08:00; run it off-peak (03:00), have it write reminder rows with their own spread times instead of enqueuing sends, and release held SMS spread over the first minutes after 08:00.

[w3] One lane at the cap is a starvation bug: a 24-hour reminder can wait an hour without harm, while a one-hour reminder is useless a few minutes late, so the sweep that still has to be built reads due rows in priority order and fills a lane per priority, with aging so the low lane still moves.

[w2] The sender is a stub that logs and answers 'accepted', so nothing yet reports provider rejections or message ids; the real adapter returns both, which gives you a 429 rate, a cost per salon, and the id to reconcile the provider's bill against.

[w1] Watch the pipeline exists before watching its speed: today no worker or sweep runs unless someone starts one, so the first alerts are a heartbeat per worker and per sweep, then queue depth and the age of the oldest due message per lane.
keyPoints.quote: so no worker or sweep runs unless you start one yourself

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your pipeline choices against the alternatives: jittered send windows versus exact send times; per-type priority lanes versus one first-in-first-out queue; a digest per salon versus one message per appointment; and buying a higher provider tier versus failover across two providers versus shedding 24-hour reminders first. For each, say what you bought and what it cost.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Jitter flattens the wave below the cap at no cost but a few minutes' precision on a one-hour reminder; exact times are easier to test and explain, but make capacity equal to the single worst instant of the week.
keyPoints.quote: confirmation now, reminders at T-24h and T-1h

keyPoints.text: [w3] Lanes protect imminent messages when behind, at the cost of more queues to watch and starvation unless the low lane ages up; today there is one queue with one job name, which is fair and simple until the cap is reached.

[w2] A digest fits the salon side (one morning schedule per staff member instead of an alert per booking) and cuts paid volume, but each customer still needs their own reminder; it is also a new message type, since every type today is about a single appointment.

[w3] A higher tier is one contract change but pays for the peak all month; a second provider covers outages as well as caps, at the cost of a second adapter, templates, deliverability reputation and per-provider message ids; shedding 24-hour reminders first under pressure is free and protects the messages that matter, provided the shed rows are recorded, not silently dropped.

[w2] Holding SMS until 08:00 respects quiet hours but builds a morning wave; switching quiet-hour sends to email avoids the wave, at lower read rates, and needs the address and the customer's zone on hand for every row.
